title: Reading Groups in Real Time
hook: In a group the most important body is rarely the one talking; watch where the eyes go when a decision gets close.
why:
Almost everything in this book so far has been taught one person at a time: one baseline, one cluster, one hypothesis. Much of life does not come one person at a time. It comes in meetings of eight, dinners of six, families of five, and the reading that matters is often not about any single person but about the group: who it is really listening to, where it is heading, who is being left out, and whether it is about to admit you or close ranks.

Groups have their own structure, and some of it is well studied. People arrange their bodies around a shared space. They pass the floor by rules so quick that nobody notices them. They look at speakers and at power in measurable patterns. This chapter teaches you to read that structure in real time: the shape of a group, the flow of its attention, its turn-taking, the signals of hierarchy and alignment, and how to sample a room you cannot possibly watch in full. It ends where it should, with your own place in the group, because you are never only watching it.

teach.h: A group has a body too.
teach.p:
Watch any party from a balcony and you will see people standing in small clusters, each roughly a circle, each with its members turned towards a shared patch of floor. The anthropologist Adam Kendon called these arrangements F-formations. When two or more people talk standing up, they tend to position themselves so that each has equal, direct access to the space between them, which he called the o-space. Their bodies form a ring around it, and the space outside the ring is where newcomers wait.

The shape tells you things before anyone speaks. A tight ring with shoulders closed means a conversation that is, for now, closed. A ring with a gap, one person standing slightly back or angled outward, is an opening: people who join a group almost always enter through such gaps. When someone is about to leave, their lower body usually turns first, feet and hips swinging away while the head stays with the conversation. When the topic becomes private, the ring tightens and voices drop.

Seated groups follow the same logic, though the furniture fixes much of it. Notice who has turned their chair, who has pushed back from the table, who has angled towards one neighbour and away from another. A meeting of eight around a table often contains two or three smaller rings, visible in the angles of torsos.

As always, the reading is of change against baseline, and the group has a baseline of its own. Some teams always sit loosely. Some friends always stand close. The useful signal is the moment a group's shape changes: the ring that tightens when a certain name comes up, the gap that opens when you approach.

Before you join a group, look at its shape. It will usually tell you whether you are welcome yet.
teach.disconfirm: If you approach standing groups through their gaps and through their closed sides about equally often, and are admitted just as readily either way, the formation is not telling you much in your setting. Track twenty approaches before deciding.

teach.h: Follow the eyes, not the voice.
teach.p:
In a group conversation, listeners mostly look at whoever is speaking, and speakers look most at the person they are addressing. That much is predictable and tells you little. The useful information is in the exceptions: the moments when listeners look away from the speaker, and where they look instead.

When a decision approaches, people look at the person they expect to make it. A proposal is put to the room, and before anyone answers, eyes go to one face. That face belongs to the real decision-maker for this question, who may or may not be the most senior person present and may not have spoken at all. The same thing happens after a joke, when people check one person's reaction before laughing fully, and after bad news, when they look to whoever will have to deal with it.

This is why the most important body in a group is rarely the one talking. The speaker has the floor. The person everyone glances at has the power over what happens next, and in many meetings those are different people.

To read this you need to stop watching the speaker at exactly the moments when the speaker is most interesting: the end of a proposal, the punchline, the announcement. At those moments, take a quick look round the room instead. You are looking for a convergence of gazes, three or four people glancing at the same face within a second or two. One person's glance means little. A convergence is a strong clue about the group's structure on this question.

Then test it, as with any reading, by watching the next decision point and seeing whether the eyes go to the same place.
teach.disconfirm: If across several decision points the listeners' glances scatter rather than converge, or converge on whoever happens to be speaking, this group has no single centre of power on these questions, or its members hide it well. Do not invent one.
teach.pullQuote: The speaker has the floor. The person everyone glances at has the power over what happens next.

teach.h: Turn-taking is a machine you can watch.
teach.p:
In 1974 Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson described the rules by which conversation passes from one speaker to the next. The current speaker can select the next one, by name, by gaze or by a question aimed at someone. If nobody is selected, the first person to start speaking gets the turn. If nobody starts, the current speaker may go on. The system runs so fast that most people never notice it. In 2009 Tanya Stivers and colleagues measured the gaps between questions and answers in ten languages around the world. In all of them, most answers began within about half a second, with Japanese speakers leaving the shortest gaps and Danish speakers the longest.

Because the system is so fast, the signals of wanting a turn are small and easy to miss. A person preparing to speak often takes a quick breath in, shifts forward, lifts a hand slightly from the table, or opens their mouth and closes it again. Watch for someone who does this two or three times without getting the floor. They are being passed over, and the group is losing whatever they had to say.

Turn-taking also shows structure. Notice who is selected by gaze most often, who is interrupted and by whom, and who takes the floor after a silence. Interruptions that run in one direction more than the other are a pattern worth recording. So is the person who is never selected but always speaks when they choose to.

There is some evidence that the distribution of turns matters to how well a group works. In 2010 Anita Woolley and her colleagues found that groups whose members took more equal turns did better across a range of tasks. Later work has questioned how strong the effect is, but the pattern is worth watching in your own meetings.
teach.disconfirm: If, when you count, the turns in a group you know turn out to be spread fairly evenly and nobody's attempts to speak go unanswered, your impression that someone is being shut out was not supported. Count again in a different meeting before revising your view of the group.

teach.h: Power shows in how people look.
teach.p:
In the 1970s Ralph Exline, Steve Ellyson and Barbara Long described a pattern they called the visual dominance ratio: the amount a person looks at their partner while speaking, divided by the amount they look while listening. Most people look more while listening than while speaking. People in positions of power tend to look about as much while speaking as while listening, which gives them a ratio near one. People in lower positions look much more while listening, which gives them a lower ratio.

John Dovidio and Steve Ellyson found in 1982 that observers use this pattern to judge power, even without being told what to look for. And in 1988 Dovidio and colleagues showed that it follows situational power rather than fixed traits. In mixed pairs of men and women, whoever held the expertise on the topic under discussion showed the higher ratio, whichever sex they were.

In a group, this gives you a second way of seeing hierarchy. Notice who holds steady eye contact while they speak, and who looks down or away when speaking but watches closely when listening. Notice the person who looks at others while they talk without seeming to seek their approval. And notice when the pattern shifts: a junior who starts to hold the room's gaze while speaking, or a senior who suddenly watches others more closely while they talk.

The usual cautions apply with extra force. Gaze norms differ between cultures. Many autistic people look less at faces whatever their status. Some people look down to think. Use the ratio as one clue about the structure of a room, never as a judgment about any single person, and always against that person's baseline.
teach.disconfirm: If the people you would rank as most powerful in a group do not show a higher ratio of looking while speaking to looking while listening, the pattern does not hold in that group, or your ranking is wrong. Check the ranking by watching who decides.

teach.p:
People in conversation tend to fall into step. They share postures, echo each other's gestures, match pace and pitch, often without knowing it. In classrooms in the 1970s Marianne LaFrance found that posture sharing between teacher and students went along with students' ratings of rapport. In 1999 Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh described what they called the chameleon effect: people unconsciously mimicked the mannerisms of a stranger they worked with, and in one study participants whose mannerisms were mimicked by a confederate liked that person more.

These findings became popular, and the popular version outran the evidence. Later studies have found the link between mimicry and liking smaller and less consistent than the first reports suggested, and some, using carefully controlled virtual characters, found no effect on rapport at all. Alignment is real. Its meaning is less certain than the advice books claim.

In a group, alignment is most useful as a map of sub-groups rather than as a measure of liking. Notice who shares posture with whom, who turns towards whom when they laugh, and who moves together, sitting back or leaning in at the same moment, when a point is made. Two or three people who repeatedly align may be allies on this question, or old friends, or simply tired at the same time. Hold the map loosely, and check it against what people actually say and decide.

One use of this knowledge is ruled out. Mimicking someone in order to win them over is the manipulation this book refuses to teach, and given the evidence, it may not even work.
teach.disconfirm: If people you map as aligned regularly take opposite sides when a decision is made, alignment is not tracking alliance in this group. Keep it as a description of who moves together, and stop reading more into it.

teach.h: Sample a room you cannot fully watch.
teach.p:
You cannot watch eight people at once, and trying to do so produces a blur in which you notice nobody. A group is read by sampling: choosing whom to watch and when, and accepting that most of the room will go unobserved most of the time.

Choose anchors. In most meetings three people repay attention more than the rest: the person who will decide, the quietest person, and the person with the most at stake in the outcome, who may be neither of the first two. Rotate your attention among them, a few seconds each, and let the rest of the room sit in your peripheral vision. Peripheral vision is poor at detail but good at movement, so it will still catch the large changes, someone pushing back from the table or turning away.

Choose moments. Some moments are worth more than others: the start, when baselines are set; the moment a proposal is put; bad news; a joke; and the end, when people relax and show what they were holding. At those moments, take a quick look round the whole room rather than staying with your anchors.

Write down what you saw as soon as you can, by anchor and by moment, rather than as an impression of the room. *At the price, Grace looked at the window and Paul looked at Grace* is a record. *The room was against it* is a story.

Accept the gaps. A sampled room is a partial picture, and the honest journal entry says which parts you saw and which you did not. Nobody reads a whole group. Good readers know which parts of it they missed.
teach.disconfirm: If, after a meeting, your sampled notes miss the change that turned out to matter, check whether it came from someone outside your anchors or at a moment you did not sample. Adjust the anchors before deciding that sampling does not work for you.

teach.h: You are part of the group you are reading.
teach.p:
Everything in this chapter so far treats you as an observer. You are never only that. Your gaze selects speakers, your posture joins or leaves the ring, your laughter tells the room whose joke landed. In a group, reading and acting cannot be separated, and the more power you hold in the room, the larger your effect on what you are trying to read.

This is a responsibility and an opportunity. If you lead a meeting, you allocate turns with your eyes whether you mean to or not. Speakers tend to look at the people they expect to answer, and the people they look at are more likely to speak. Use that deliberately. When you notice someone who has tried to come in and failed, look at them at the next pause, and if needed say their name: *Tomasz, you were about to say something.* It costs a second and often changes the outcome.

Notice too what your own body is doing to the group's baseline. If you are tense, the room will often tighten around you, and you may then read the tightness as something about them. If you are the senior person and you lean back and go quiet, others may wait for you, and their waiting can look like reluctance.

Before you trust a group reading, ask what part of it you caused. Then test it in a way that does not depend on you, for example by asking an open question of the whole room and watching who answers first, or by checking with individuals afterwards, one at a time, in private.

Read the group, then the person, then yourself in both.
teach.disconfirm: If the patterns you see in a group stay the same whether you are present, absent, leading or simply attending, your effect on that group is small. A colleague's notes from a meeting you missed are the simplest way to check.

poseGallery.doCaption: Both bodies still turned towards the shared space.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Talking on while the other's body has already turned to leave.
poseGallery.annotation: Feet and hips usually swing away before the head does. The lower body announces a departure first.

poseGallery.doCaption: Watching where the listeners look as the decision approaches.
poseGallery.annotation: The speaker has the floor; the person everyone glances at has the power. Look round the room at the moments that matter.

poseGallery.doCaption: Noticing who aligns with whom, and leaving it at that.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Mirroring someone's posture to win him over.
poseGallery.annotation: Alignment is real, but its link to liking is weaker than the advice books claim, and using it as a technique is manipulation.

poseGallery.doCaption: Using your gaze to hand the floor to someone who has been trying to speak.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Holding the floor with your eyes on the most senior person.
poseGallery.annotation: Gaze allocates turns. Whoever leads a group decides, often without noticing, who gets heard.

poseGallery.doCaption: Waiting at the gap until the ring opens
poseGallery.dontCaption: Walking straight into a closed ring
poseGallery.annotation: People join groups through gaps. A closed ring is usually about its conversation, not about you.

caseStudy:
Sam, thirty-three, has just become a project manager at an engineering firm, and his first big meeting is a supplier decision. Seven people sit round the table. Paul, the operations director, talks most and talks with confidence: the cheaper supplier is the obvious choice. Sam assumes the decision is Paul's.

He has decided in advance to sample rather than stare, so his anchors are Paul, the quietest person in the room, and whoever has most at stake. The quietest is Grace, head of finance, at the far end of the table. She has said almost nothing. When Paul puts the proposal to the room and asks whether anyone objects, Sam looks round instead of at Paul. Four people glance at Grace within a second. So does Paul. Grace's pen has stopped, and she is looking at the window.

Sam also notices Tomasz, a junior engineer, who has leaned forward and taken a quick breath three times during the discussion, and each time been talked over. The fourth time, Sam looks at him and says, *Tomasz, you were about to say something.* Tomasz says that the cheaper supplier's site failed an inspection last spring.

Sam turns to Grace. *What would you need to see before you were comfortable?* She says she would want the inspection report and three years of the supplier's accounts. The decision is deferred for a fortnight.

Afterwards Sam writes his notes by anchor and moment, not as an impression. He later learns that every contract above a certain value needs Grace's signature, which nobody had mentioned to a new manager. At the next decision meeting he watches the eyes again. They go to Grace. When the inspection report arrives, the firm chooses the other supplier.
observe: In your next group conversation, notice where the listeners' eyes go just before a decision, an answer to a proposal, or a laugh.
In a public place, briefly watch a few groups of three or more people standing together, and notice the shape each makes and whether it has an opening.
In a meeting, notice one person who tries to speak and does not get the floor, and what they did each time just before giving up.

drills.name: Eye Map
steps: In a meeting or a recorded panel discussion, sketch where each person sits.
At three moments, the start, a proposal and a decision or answer, mark with an arrow where each person is looking.
Note who received the most glances at the decision moment and who spoke the most overall.
Compare both with the formal roles in the room.
Write one hypothesis about the group's structure on this question, and the next decision point at which you will test it.
variations: Do the eye map on a recording with the sound off, and see whether you can tell from the glances alone when a decision point arrives.
Map the same team in three meetings with different agendas, and note whether the person receiving the glances changes with the topic.
Compare your map with a colleague who attended the same meeting, without discussing it first.

drills.name: Turn Ledger
steps: Choose a recorded discussion of three or more people lasting at least fifteen minutes.
Tally the turns each person takes.
Mark each interruption with an arrow from the interrupter to the person interrupted.
Mark each failed attempt to speak, such as a breath, a lean forward or a half-started word that did not get the floor.
Write down what the tallies show that you did not notice while simply watching.
variations: Keep the ledger on a recording of a family or friends' dinner scene in a film, and compare the pattern with a recorded business meeting.
Add a column for who speaks first after each silence, and see whether it is the same person most of the time.
Keep a ledger on one of your own recorded video calls, and include yourself in the tally.

drills.name: Formation Watch
steps: In a public place such as a station concourse, a park or a reception, choose five standing groups to observe briefly, never staring.
Sketch the shape of each group, marking any gaps in the ring.
For each, predict with a percentage whether it will admit a newcomer or break up within five minutes.
Check each prediction from a distance as it resolves.
Record your hit rate and which features of the shape you relied on.
variations: Repeat the drill in a different kind of setting, such as a conference coffee break, and compare which features of the shape you relied on.
Watch for groups that are about to break up, and note whether the lower body turns before the head, as the chapter describes.
Predict which group a newcomer will join, rather than whether a group will admit someone, and check from a distance.

drills.name: Sampling Rotation
steps: Before a meeting, choose three anchors: the person who will decide, the quietest person, and the person with most at stake.
During the meeting, rotate your attention among the anchors every few seconds, leaving the rest to peripheral vision.
At the start, at any proposal and at the end, look round the whole room once.
Afterwards, write what each anchor did at each key moment, as behaviour rather than impressions.
Note one thing you saw that you would have missed watching only the speakers.
variations: Change one anchor halfway through the meeting, and note what you see in the new anchor that you had missed.
Use only peripheral vision for the rest of the room, and write down every movement it caught that turned out to matter.
Ask a colleague to sample the same meeting with different anchors, and compare your two records afterwards.

drills.name: Give the Floor
steps: In a meeting you lead or attend, watch for one person who tries to speak and is passed over.
At the next pause, look at them, and if needed say their name and invite them in.
Note what they say and how the discussion changes.
Repeat in at least two more meetings over the next fortnight.
Write down what you learned in those meetings that you would otherwise not have heard.
variations: When you invite someone in, offer a way out, such as asking whether they have anything to add or are happy to pass, and note the difference.
Ask the person afterwards, privately, whether being invited in was welcome, and adjust how you do it next time.
Try handing the floor with your gaze alone, without saying a name, and record how often it works.

quiz.q: In a meeting, who usually tells you the most about where a decision is going?
options: Whoever is speaking, since they hold the attention of everyone in the room
The most senior person on the organisation chart, whatever happens in the room
Whoever the listeners glance at as the decision gets close
Whoever has spoken the most often and for the longest during the meeting
quiz.explain: The speaker holds the floor, but the face the listeners check as a decision approaches belongs to whoever they expect to decide. That is often not the speaker, and sometimes not the most senior person present.

quiz.q: In Adam Kendon's account of F-formations, what does the shape of a standing group tell you?
options: Whether the members share a space for talk, and whether it is open
Which member of the group holds the highest status at work or in the family
How long the members of the group have known each other, roughly in years
Whether the members like each other or are only being polite for now
quiz.explain: People talking together arrange themselves around a shared space they all have access to. A closed ring signals a closed conversation; a gap is usually where newcomers enter. Shape says little on its own about status or liking.

quiz.q: What is the visual dominance ratio?
options: The share of a meeting during which a particular person holds the floor
Looking while speaking, divided by looking while listening
The number of people in the room who look at someone while he speaks
How often a person is the first to break eye contact in a conversation
quiz.explain: People with more situational power tend to look about as much while speaking as while listening; those with less look much more while listening. It is a clue about a room's structure, never a verdict on one person, and gaze norms vary by culture and person.

quiz.q: Two colleagues sit with mirrored postures through most of a meeting. What can you reasonably conclude?
options: That they agree with each other on the main issue being discussed
That one of them is deliberately mimicking the other to win his trust
That they are friends outside work and have known each other for years
Only a weak hypothesis that they are aligned, to check against what they do
quiz.explain: Alignment is real, but its link to liking and agreement is weaker and less consistent than early studies suggested. Use it as a map of who moves together, and check it against what people say and decide.

quiz.q: What did Tanya Stivers and colleagues find when they measured turn-taking in ten languages?
options: Most answers began within about half a second in every language
Gaps between turns differed by several seconds from language to language
Only European languages showed any regular pattern of taking turns
Speakers of most languages talked over each other most of the time
quiz.explain: Turn-taking was fast everywhere, with modest differences between languages. Because the system is so quick, the signs of someone wanting a turn are small, and someone repeatedly passed over is easy to miss.

quiz.q: You are leading a meeting and notice a junior colleague lean forward and take a quick breath three times without getting a word in. What fits?
options: Leave it, since he will speak up when he has something important enough to say
Look at him at the next pause and invite him in by name
Mention it to him privately after the meeting so that he can be more assertive
Ask the group to raise hands before speaking for the rest of the meeting
quiz.explain: Those are classic signs of a failed attempt to take a turn. As the leader you allocate turns with your gaze whether you mean to or not, so a look and his name at the next pause is quick and often changes what the group hears.

quiz.q: What did Dovidio and his colleagues find in 1988 about the visual dominance ratio in mixed pairs of men and women?
options: That men always showed the higher ratio, whatever the topic being discussed
That women always showed the higher ratio, because they look more while listening
That whoever held the expertise on the topic showed the higher ratio, whichever sex they were
That the ratio was the same for everyone and showed nothing about power at all
quiz.explain: Visual dominance followed situational power, such as expertise on the topic, rather than fixed traits. That is why a convergence of glances is a clue about the structure of a group on one question, not a fixed fact about a person.

quiz.q: At a party, you see a group of three standing close in a tight ring, shoulders angled in, voices low. What fits this chapter best?
options: Look for another group with a gap in its ring, and do not read this one's closed shape as being about you
Walk up and stand right next to them, since the ring will open once they notice you standing there
Decide that the people at this party are cliquey, since a closed ring shows they do not want newcomers
Interrupt with a friendly question, since a confident opening is the best way to break into a group
quiz.explain: A tight ring with shoulders closed is a conversation that is closed for now, often for its own reasons, such as a private topic. People join groups through gaps, so the better move is to find a group that has one.

quiz.q: Someone tells you that mirroring a person's posture will make them like you, because research has proved it. What does the chapter say?
options: That the research shows mirroring always works, provided the other person does not notice that you are doing it
That later studies found the link smaller and less consistent, and that mimicry to win people over is ruled out here
That mirroring has been shown to make people dislike you, so you should always adopt the opposite posture to theirs
That posture sharing has never been studied, so nobody can say whether it means anything at all
quiz.explain: Chartrand and Bargh's early findings were influential, but later work found the effect smaller and less consistent, and some studies found none. Whatever the evidence, mimicking people to win them over is the manipulation this book refuses to teach.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific group you belong to that meets regularly, such as a team, a family or a group of friends. Who speaks most? Who do people look at when a decision is close? Are those the same person? Describe one moment you remember when the group's attention went somewhere you did not expect, and say what you would watch for at the next meeting to test your picture of how this group really works.
reflection.guidance: Most people find that the person who speaks most and the person the group defers to are different more often than they expected, especially in families. If you cannot remember where eyes went at decision points, that is the first thing to watch for. Be careful to describe the group's structure, not to judge any one person in it.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to watch the speaker, which is natural and tells you least. The second is the opposite: reading hierarchy into every glance and building a confident organisation chart from a single meeting, ignoring culture, personal style, and the person who simply looked at the clock. The third is trying to watch everyone and seeing no one. The fourth is misusing what you learn: mirroring people to win them over, choosing seats to dominate, steering turns to shut out a rival. And the most constant failure is forgetting that you are in the group. Your gaze, your posture and your silence shape what you are trying to read, so test group readings in ways that do not depend on you.

moreCases.title: The family dinner where the eyes went to the youngest
moreCases.scene:
Nadia, thirty-six, has been married into her husband's family for nine years. Six months after her father-in-law's death, the family gathers for Sunday lunch to discuss whether to sell his house. Imran, forty-four, the eldest son, does most of the talking. He has spoken to an estate agent, he has figures, and he says that selling soon is the sensible thing to do. Nobody argues.

Nadia, who has no say in the decision and knows it, watches the table instead of Imran. When he finishes and asks, *So, are we agreed?*, three people glance at Sana, thirty, the youngest sister, within a second. So does Nadia's husband. Sana, who usually talks more than anyone at these lunches, has said almost nothing. Her fork has stopped, and she is looking at her plate.

Imran takes the silence as agreement and starts talking about dates. Sana nods once, without looking up. Nadia notices that Sana's chair has moved back from the table since the start of the meal, and that her husband, sitting beside Sana, has angled himself towards her.

Sana lives ten minutes from the house. For the last two years of their father's life, she was the one who visited every day.

Imran had arranged the lunch, chosen the date and brought the estate agent's letter. Nobody had asked Sana whether it was a good day for her.
moreCases.misread:
Imran read the silence round the table as agreement and Sana's single nod as consent. He was watching the speaker, himself, and the people he expected to argue. The convergence of glances told a different story: on this question, the room was waiting for Sana.

Imran also read his own figures as the heart of the matter, when for at least one person at the table the house was not mainly about money.
moreCases.betterRead:
The eyes showed where the decision really sat, and Sana's body showed a change from her baseline at the moment the decision was put: silence from the most talkative person at the table, a stopped fork, a chair pushed back. None of that said what Sana felt, and Nadia, as an in-law, had no standing to announce a reading. What she could do was small. She said, lightly, *Does it have to be decided today? It's a big thing.* Two people visibly relaxed. Imran agreed to wait a month. Later, in the kitchen, Nadia asked Sana how she was finding it all, and Sana cried for the first time since the funeral.

Nadia never told anyone what she had noticed at the table. She did not need to.

What Nadia had read was not Sana's feelings but the room's structure: who the decision belonged to, and that she had not yet been asked. Her one sentence did nothing more than make room for the question.

moreCases.title: The volunteer who thought the room was cliquey
moreCases.scene:
Ama, fifty-eight, has just retired from nursing and joined a group of volunteers who run a community garden. At their summer social, held in a church hall, she knows almost nobody. She takes a drink and tries to join a conversation.

The first group she approaches is two women standing close, shoulders angled together, speaking quietly. Ama stands beside them and smiles. They smile back briefly, but the ring does not open, and after a minute she moves away. The second group is three men talking about football in a tight triangle. One glances at her and then back. The third is a couple who are plainly about to leave; their feet are already pointing at the door. By now Ama has decided that the group is cliquey and that she will not come again.

On her way to get her coat, she passes a group of four in a loose ring by the tea urn. One man is standing slightly back from the others, angled outward, with a gap beside him. He catches her eye.

She later learns that the two women in the first group were talking about one of them's recent bereavement.

She had spent thirty years reading patients on wards and had never felt so unable to read a room, which made the evening feel worse than it was.
moreCases.misread:
Ama read three closed rings, one after the other, as a verdict on her and on the group. Each was a closed conversation, for its own reasons: a private topic, an established triangle, a couple leaving. None was about her.

She read the man who caught her eye at the urn, at first, as another polite brush-off, and had almost walked past before she noticed the gap beside him.
moreCases.betterRead:
Kendon's F-formations make the difference readable before anyone speaks. A tight ring with shoulders closed is a conversation that is closed for now, and people who join groups almost always enter through gaps. The group by the urn was the open one: loose, with a member angled outward and a space beside him. Ama stood at the gap and waited, and the man stepped back to let her in. Within ten minutes she had been asked to help with the autumn planting. The rule she took away was simple. Look at the shape first. If a ring does not open, move on without reading it as rejection, because it is usually about the conversation rather than you.

At the next social she found the two women from the first group, who greeted her warmly and apologised for having been distracted.

She also noticed, over the next few months, that the people who stood slightly apart at these events were often the ones who had joined most recently, and she started standing that way herself, to leave a gap for whoever came next.

moreCases.title: The chair who caused the silence she read
moreCases.scene:
Helen, fifty-two, chairs the governing board of a primary school. She has read the chapter on groups and has resolved to talk less in meetings and let others speak, since she knows that as chair she tends to dominate. At the spring meeting the head teacher presents a proposal to change the start of the school day. Helen leans back, folds her hands and says nothing.

Nobody else says anything either. The silence lasts several seconds, then a few more. Two governors glance at Helen. The vice-chair looks at his papers. Helen reads the room as reluctant, and wonders whether the proposal is in trouble. When someone finally speaks, it is to ask a small question about the buses. Helen, worried that the board is unconvinced, suggests deferring the decision to the next meeting.

Afterwards, the vice-chair stops her in the car park. He says that everyone was waiting to hear what she thought, as they always do, and that when she said nothing, they assumed she had doubts and did not want to say so in front of the head. He had been in favour himself, and so, he thinks, had most of the board.

At previous meetings Helen had always opened discussion by saying what she thought, and nobody had ever remarked on it.
moreCases.misread:
Helen read the silence as the board's reluctance. Much of it was produced by her own change of behaviour: the person the room always looked to had leaned back and gone quiet, and the room read her silence as a signal and waited. The glances at her were the clue she missed.

She also read the question about the buses as a sign of doubt, when it was simply the first thing anyone felt safe to say.

She had read her own silence as neutral, as if a chair could disappear from the room by saying nothing.
moreCases.betterRead:
You are part of the group you are reading, and the more power you hold in it, the larger your effect. A chair who suddenly goes silent changes the group's baseline, and the room's waiting can look exactly like reluctance. The test Helen needed was one that did not depend on her: an open question to the whole room, such as *I'd like to hear from everyone before I say what I think. What are your views?*, and then a slow round of the table. At the next meeting she did exactly that, and said so in advance. The proposal passed with one abstention, and two governors raised points about the buses that improved it.

She also told the board, in advance of the next meeting, that she would speak last.

The vice-chair's word in the car park was the test that did not depend on her, and it was the one that told her the truth. It was also, she realised, the kind of thing people only say to a chair afterwards and in private.

moreCases.title: The consultant who drew an organisation chart from one meeting
moreCases.scene:
Daniel, twenty-nine, is a management consultant at the start of a project with a manufacturing client. In the first meeting, with eight of the client's managers, he practises the eye map from this chapter. Several times, when a question is put to the room, three or four people glance at Rachel, forty, a manager whose title he has not quite caught. The managing director talks most, but the eyes go to Rachel.

That evening Daniel writes to his own director: *The real power in this room is Rachel. The MD defers to her. We should focus our stakeholder work on her.* He is pleased with the reading, which feels like exactly the kind of thing the chapter teaches.

At the second meeting, a week later, the agenda is different. The questions are about strategy, and when they are put to the room, the eyes go to the managing director, every time. Rachel barely speaks. Daniel's director asks him, gently, what Rachel's job is. Daniel checks. She is the finance manager. Most of the questions in the first meeting were about costs, and she had brought the figures and was controlling the slides on the screen.

Daniel's director had asked him to keep his notes on the client to behaviour and roles, and to check his impressions with the team before writing them up.
moreCases.misread:
Daniel read a convergence of glances in one meeting as a fixed fact about the organisation. The glances were real, but they were about the question, the figures and the screen: people looked at the person who held the numbers for that agenda.

He also read the managing director's talking as deference to Rachel, when it was simply his style in every meeting.
moreCases.betterRead:
A convergence of gazes is a strong clue about the group's structure *on this question*, and the chapter's caution is in those last words. Dovidio's work points the same way: visual dominance follows situational power, such as expertise on the topic, rather than fixed rank. People look at the person who controls the screen, whose department the topic concerns, or who is expected to know the facts. One meeting gives you a hypothesis, to be tested at the next decision point on a different kind of question. The cheapest test of all is to ask how decisions are made. Daniel's director had simply asked the managing director, at the start, who needed to sign off on the project.

Daniel's note to his director was withdrawn. The stakeholder work began with the managing director.

Rachel turned out to be important to the project after all, as the person whose figures every recommendation would have to survive, but that was a different reading, and it came from asking.

workedReading.title: An eye map and turn ledger on a recorded panel
workedReading.scene:
Leah, thirty-one, is practising the eye map and turn ledger on a twenty-minute recording of a local television panel about whether to close a branch library. There are four guests and a presenter. The guests are the leader of the council, a man of about sixty; a campaigner for the library, a woman of about forty-five; the owner of a local business, a man of about fifty; and a young teacher, a woman in her late twenties. Leah has paper, a pen and a rule: no conclusions until she has written down what she saw at each moment. She also reminds herself that the recording is edited, and that the director, not she, chose which faces were on screen.

She has chosen a panel because it is unscripted and because the people on it chose to be filmed, which makes it fair material for practice.

Her aim is not to judge any of the guests but to practise seeing the structure of a group she has no stake in.

steps.label: Sketch the seats
steps.text:
She pauses on the first wide shot and sketches the layout. The guests sit in a shallow arc facing the presenter, with the council leader and the business owner on one side and the campaigner and the teacher on the other. The presenter sits at the end nearest the council leader. Leah notes that the seating may have been chosen by the producers to put the two sides opposite each other, so the arrangement itself tells her about the programme rather than the people.

She also notes the camera positions: one wide shot from behind the presenter and close-ups of whoever is speaking.

steps.label: Set the group baseline
steps.text:
In the first three minutes, the introductions, everyone looks at the presenter while she speaks, and each guest looks at her while answering. The council leader sits back with one arm on the chair. The campaigner sits forward with her hands together. The business owner sits still. The teacher sits upright and nods slightly while others speak. Leah writes these down as the baselines for this setting, for each of them, before anything contentious has been said.

She notes that the campaigner's forward lean is her baseline here, not a sign of anything, since she held it before any question had been asked.

steps.label: Tally turns and attempts
steps.text:
Over the twenty minutes Leah tallies the turns. The council leader takes eleven, the campaigner nine, the business owner six and the teacher three. She marks the interruptions with arrows: four in all, three of them by the council leader, each time cutting off the campaigner. She also marks failed attempts to speak, and finds five by the teacher: a quick breath in, a lean forward, once a half-started word, each time without getting the floor.

She notes that the teacher's three turns all came when the presenter selected her by name, never by taking the floor herself.

The ledger shows what simply watching had not: the teacher had tried to speak more often than anyone except the council leader, and had been heard least.

steps.label: Watch the eyes at the question
steps.text:
At minute twelve the presenter asks, *So, will the library close?* Leah rewinds and watches the wide shot frame by frame. The campaigner and the business owner both glance at the council leader before he answers, and so does the teacher. The council leader looks at the presenter, not the guests. On this question the convergence goes where the formal roles would predict. Leah notes that not every reading is a surprise, and that a reading which confirms the obvious is still worth recording.

She also notices that the business owner glances at the council leader a second time, after his answer, and writes it down without deciding what it means.

steps.label: Map the alignments
steps.text:
Leah notices that the council leader and the business owner sit back at the same moment twice, and that the campaigner and the teacher lean in together when the teacher finally speaks. She writes this down as a possible map of two sub-groups on this question, and holds it loosely. They may be allies, they may have been seated to look like it, or they may simply be reacting to the same moments in the same way. Their words will settle it better than their postures.

She checks the transcript afterwards and finds that the business owner and the council leader disagree on two points, which makes the ally reading weaker than the postures suggested.

steps.label: Test at the next decision
steps.text:
At minute seventeen the presenter asks whether a local business might fund the library to keep it open. This time the eyes go to the business owner: the council leader looks at him, and so does the campaigner. He sits forward for the first time. Leah writes that power on this panel seems to follow the question, as Dovidio's work suggests: the council leader for the decision, the business owner for the money. One panel is not enough to say more.

She also notices that the teacher is selected more often in the last five minutes, after the presenter has looked at her twice, which looks like a presenter handing over the floor deliberately.

steps.label: Write it as record
steps.text:
Her final notes are by moment, not impression: *At 'will it close?', three of three guests looked at the council leader. At the funding question, two looked at the business owner, who sat forward. Teacher: five failed attempts to speak, three turns.* She also writes down what she could not see: the teacher's hands, which were out of shot for most of the programme, and any reactions the editor cut. The record is partial, and it says so.

She writes one hypothesis to test on a second episode of the same programme: that the presenter hands the floor to quieter guests near the end.

moreFailures.title: Reading the room from its most expressive member
moreFailures.body:
In most groups one or two people show their reactions far more than the rest. They laugh loudest, frown most visibly and sigh audibly at the agenda. It is easy to treat them as the room's barometer and read the group's mood from their faces alone. But expressive people are expressive whatever the group thinks, and their reactions say more about their own style than about anyone else's view. A room in which one person groans at a proposal may be broadly in favour of it; a room in which one person laughs may be quietly unimpressed. Read the expressive member against their own baseline, like anyone else, and use the anchors and the room-wide glance at key moments to see whether others are with them. The quiet majority is usually where the group's real position lies.

It is also worth noticing who reacts after the expressive member, rather than at the same time. The people who check that member's face before reacting may be following them; the people who do not are showing you something of their own.

moreFailures.title: Reading gaze on a video call as if it were a room
moreFailures.body:
On a video call, nobody can look at anybody in particular. Each person sees a grid of faces, and their eyes go to the screen, to the camera or to their notes, in ways that bear no relation to who they are attending to. The convergence of gazes, the visual dominance ratio and the shape of the ring are all lost or scrambled. Readers who carry the room rules onto a screen will see patterns that do not exist, such as a colleague who seems to be avoiding the boss's eye because her camera is above a second monitor. On calls, rely on what still carries information: who unmutes first after a question, who speaks after a silence, who uses the chat, whose camera goes off, and above all the answers to direct questions put to people by name.

Part IV's chapters on video calls cover this in more detail.

A face on a call looking down may be reading the chat, checking a document or watching another person's video, and you will not know which.

moreFailures.title: Rescuing someone who did not want the floor
moreFailures.body:
Giving the floor to someone who has tried and failed to speak is one of the most useful things this chapter teaches. Done carelessly, it can also embarrass people who were content to listen. A quiet member is not always someone being shut out. Some people prefer to think before they speak, some speak only when they have something specific to add, and some find being named in front of a group acutely uncomfortable. Before you invite someone in, look for the signs of a failed attempt, a breath, a lean forward, a half-started word, rather than simple quietness. When you invite, offer a way out: *Anything to add, or happy to pass for now?* And if the setting allows, ask afterwards, in private, whether there was anything they wanted to say.

In some cultures and settings, being singled out to speak is far more uncomfortable than in others, which is one more reason to ask lightly.

Remember, too, that you are part of the group. A senior person inviting a junior to speak is a stronger act than an equal doing the same, and it can feel more like being called on in class.

moreFailures.title: Counting turns as if more were always better
moreFailures.body:
A turn ledger can make inequality vivid, and it is tempting to conclude that every meeting should give everyone the same number of turns. Woolley's finding that more equal turn-taking went with better group performance has been questioned by later work, and even where it holds, it is a pattern across groups rather than a rule for any one meeting. Some people have more to contribute on a particular question than others, and a meeting about the budget may rightly be dominated by the person who holds it. The useful target is narrower: nobody who wants to speak should be shut out, and the pattern of interruptions should not run consistently in one direction. Use the ledger to spot those problems, not to enforce a quota.

Counting also changes what you notice. Once you start tallying turns, you will see the quiet members more clearly, which is useful, and may start to see their quietness as a problem, which often it is not.

The ledger is a tool for noticing, not a measure of whether a meeting was good.

questions.q: How can I read a group when I am the one presenting to it?
questions.a:
With difficulty, and you should accept that. While you are speaking, most of your attention goes to what you are saying, and you are also the person everyone is looking at, which changes what you see. Build pauses into the presentation, at the points where a decision or a reaction matters, and use them to look round the room rather than at your notes. Choose two anchors in advance, usually the decision-maker and the person with most at stake, and glance at them at those pauses. Ask questions of the room rather than relying on faces. And if the occasion matters, ask a colleague you trust to sit in and watch for you, writing down what they see at each moment, since they will see far more than you can.

Afterwards, compare your colleague's notes with your own impressions. The gap between them is usually large, and it is the best measure you will get of how little a presenter sees.

questions.q: Is it rude to look round the room when somebody else is speaking?
questions.a:
Brief glances are fine, and most people do them naturally at the moments this chapter describes: the end of a proposal, a joke, bad news. What is rude is staring at anyone, and especially fixing your eyes on the person you have decided holds the power, which they and others may notice. Most of the time, look at the speaker, as everyone else does. At key moments, take one quick look round the room and return. If you are watching a recording, there is no such constraint, which is one reason this book uses recordings for practice. In live meetings, sampling is meant to be light, a few seconds here and there, not continuous surveillance of the room.

If someone does notice you watching them, look away naturally and return your attention to the speaker.

It also helps to remember why you are looking. If the reason is to understand how the group works, a glance is enough. If it is to catch someone out, the glance has become something else.

questions.q: What should I do if I notice that one person is repeatedly being talked over?
questions.a:
If you are chairing, use the chair's power directly. At the next pause, look at them and, if needed, say their name: *You were about to say something.* If talking over has become a pattern, you can also change the process, by going round the table or asking for views in writing before the meeting. If you are not chairing, you still have some power. You can look at the person at a pause, which often hands them the floor, or say, *I'd like to hear what she was starting to say.* Afterwards, ask them privately whether that was welcome, and whether there was more they wanted to add. Do not make it a public issue about the person who interrupted unless the pattern continues, and if it does, raise it with the chair rather than in the meeting.

If you are the person being talked over, the same tools work for you: lean in and start a sentence at a pause, look at the chair, or ask to come back to your point before the item closes.

questions.q: How much of this chapter still works on video calls?
questions.a:
Some of it, and you need to know which parts. Gaze direction is almost meaningless on a call, because everyone looks at a grid or a camera rather than at each other, so the eye map and the visual dominance ratio do not transfer. The shape of the ring disappears entirely. Turn-taking survives, though it is slower and clumsier because of delay, and a turn ledger on a call can still show who is interrupted and who never gets in. Unmuting and starting to speak are the video equivalents of the breath and lean forward. Part IV's chapters on video calls go further. The main adjustment is to ask more: put questions to people by name, and do not rely on faces to tell you whether the group agrees.

On calls with cameras off, the group is even harder to read, and asking by name becomes the main tool you have.

You can also borrow the room's rules back by asking a colleague who is in the same physical room as other participants what they saw, since they can watch faces that the call hides from you.

questions.q: How do I join a group at a party or networking event without feeling awkward?
questions.a:
Look at the shape before you approach. Choose a group with a gap in its ring, or with one person standing slightly back or angled outward, and approach towards the gap rather than from behind anyone. Stop at the edge, make brief eye contact with one person and wait. Usually someone will step back to let you in within a few seconds, and the ring will widen. Listen for a minute before you speak, so that you join the conversation rather than starting a new one. If the ring does not open, move on without reading it as rejection. A closed ring is usually about the conversation it contains, and the next group may be wide open.

If you are with a friend, approach together; a pair is often admitted more easily than a single newcomer, and you have someone to talk to if the ring does not open.

It also helps to have something to offer when you are let in, such as a question about how the others know the host, which hands the floor back to them.

questions.q: Can I use this to work out who really holds power in a new workplace?
questions.a:
As hypotheses, yes, tested over several decisions of different kinds. A convergence of glances in one meeting tells you about one question on one day. If the eyes go to the same person across meetings about money, people and strategy, you have a stronger clue. But the cheapest test is usually to ask. *Who needs to sign off on this?* or *How are decisions like this usually made here?* are ordinary questions for someone new, and the answers will tell you more than an eye map. Use the eye map for what asking cannot easily reveal: whose opinion people check before they commit, and who is being consulted less than their role suggests.

Keep your hypotheses about power to yourself until they have survived several tests, and even then, use them to understand the place rather than to work round people.

A new person who reads power and then uses it to go round people quickly gets a reputation for it, and that reading will be correct.

watch.title: 12 Angry Men: These People
watch.notice: One juror launches into a prejudiced rant, and one by one the others rise and turn their backs on him. A whole group's verdict, delivered without a word.

reviewPrompt: At the next decision point in a meeting, look round the room instead of at the speaker, and note whose face the listeners check.
